heading_path: SGA: Plug&Play Geometric Verification for Educational Video Synthesis
Abstract

blocks.text: Recent work leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate executable code for pedagogical animations using libraries such as Manim. However, ensuring spatial correctness and visual legibility remains challenging, as existing frameworks emphasize pedagogical content while overlooking geometric occlusions. We propose the Symbolic Geometric Agent (SGA), a plug-and-play module for code-centric animation pipelines that intercepts LLM-generated code, performs partial execution to extract symbolic scene graphs, and applies targeted refinement when spatial conflicts are detected. We further introduce the Manim Visual Quality Score (MVQS), a deterministic rendering-free proxy for spatial integrity. Introduction

blocks.text: Video has become a dominant medium for instructional content in modern digital education. In mathematics and science, structured animations require precise spatial organization, clear visual hierarchy, and coherent temporal transitions to effectively communicate abstract concepts (Khalil et al., 2024; Navarrete et al., 2025; Clark and Mayer, 2023; Mayer, 2024). As demand for scalable educational content grows, research increasingly focuses on automating the production of explanatory videos. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled language-to-program generation, allowing natural language prompts to be translated into executable programs for visual content creation. Moving beyond direct synthesis in pixel space, emerging code-centric paradigms generate structured animation programs, such as Python scripts for the Manim engine (Developers, 2020), which are then rendered into educational videos (Chen et al., 2025). This approach offers substantial advantages in controllability, reproducibility, and semantic transparency compared to diffusion-based or pixel-level video generation (Lin et al., 2025; Shah et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026). Educational animations require strict geometric consistency, in which text does not overlap, equations remain aligned, and objects preserve their scale relationships to maintain readability. Empirical analyses of state-of-the-art code-centric systems reveal that spatial layout remains the weakest component in automated generation. For instance, Theorem- ExplainAgent reports that element layout receives the lowest evaluation scores among all assessed criteria, even when factual accuracy and logical coherence are high (Ku et al., 2025). These issues are not merely aesthetic; in educational contexts, poor spatial organization increases cognitive load and can impair knowledge transfer (Clark and Mayer, 2023; Leiker et al., 2023). Current approaches primarily rely on posthoc perceptual evaluation using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to critique rendered video frames (Chen et al., 2025). While effective for high-level assessment, VLM-based critique operates in pixel space, requires expensive full-video rendering, and produces coarse, non-deterministic feedback. blocks.text: Related Work
heading_path: SGA: Plug&Play Geometric Verification for Educational Video Synthesis
Related Work

blocks.text: Code-Centric Educational Video Generation. Traditional generative video research has largely focused on end-to-end models operating in pixel or latent spaces, including diffusion-based (Gupta et al., 2024; Ho et al., 2022; Xing et al., 2024; Lian et al., 2023) and autoregressive approaches (Deng et al., 2024; Khachatryan et al., 2023). However, such models often struggle with the long-form reasoning, controllability, and spatial consistency required for instructional content. Recent advances in large language models have enabled code-centric generation paradigms in which LLMs produce executable animation programs through multi-step reasoning and iterative refinement. Frameworks such as ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) demonstrate how language models can interleave reasoning and external actions (Shinn et al., 2023; Madaan et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2024), while specialized systems such as Code2Video (Chen et al., 2025) and TheoremExplainAgent (Ku et al., 2025) show that structured program generation enables controllable and semantically coherent educational animations. Despite these advances, current systems primarily rely on internal LLM reasoning and lack mechanisms to verify the geometric consistency of generated layouts before rendering. Our work addresses this limitation through symbolic geometric verification directly in the code generation pipeline of systems

Interception Flow

blocks.text: The SGA operates as a non-invasive verification layer, treating animation synthesis as an iterative code-space optimization problem. Given a target topic T , a generative model L produces an initial script C(0). The SGA intercepts the execution flow and executes a four-stage refinement loop at each iteration i: (1) Symbolic Extraction, where C(i) undergoes low-latency partial execution to derive a symbolic scene graph S (i), bypassing full video rendering overhead (Sec. 3.2); (2) Deterministic Conflict Detection, wherein S (i) is evaluated for spatial violations via exact Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) analysis, replacing stochastic VLM heuristics with reproducible geometric verification (Sec. 3.3); (3) Actionable Feedback, involving a compiler F that translates violations into a structured diagnostic report F (i) containing precomputed fix vectors and canonical Manim correction templates (Sec. 3.5); and (4) Targeted Refinement, where the LLM performs precise, line-level edits conditioned on the symbolic feedback: C(i+1) =L(T, C(i), F(i))(1) Refinement terminates after a fixed budget of n iterations, effectively bounding computational overhead while allowing the LLM to iteratively incorporate symbolic grounding constraints. A summarized version of the algorithm is provided in the supplemental material (Sec. 6).

To distinguish severe occlusions from incidental contact, we compute asymmetric coverage ratios ρself ij =I ij/Ai and ρother ij =I ij/Aj, where Ak =w k ×h k is the bounding box area. Conflict severity is discretized as HIGH( max(ρ)>0.30 ), MEDIUM( >0.10 ), or LOW. Semantic and Spatio-Temporal Filtering.To preserve intentional compositions, we apply a twostage filter. Stage 1 (Contextual) matches the animation description against a vocabulary of placement (e.g., “on, root”), motion (e.g., “slide”), and geometric (e.g., “axis”) keywords. Stage 2 (Structural) performs static analysis to detect patterns such as decorative enclosures (P1), annotation pointers (P2), explicit centering calls (P3), container geometries (P4), and mathematical braces (P5). Conflicts matching these patterns are treated as intentional or pedagogical and suppressed. Finally, for dynamic scenes, the SGA performs Spatio-Temporal Sampling across K= 11 frames. Conflicts at t∈ {0,1} are flagged as persistent errors requiring patches, while mid-trajectory overlaps (0< t <1 ) are classified as transient and ignored to preserve intended animation paths. blocks.text: We evaluate SGA as a plug-and-play spatial verification layer for educational video generation. The agent is integrated into two SOTA frameworks: TheoremExplainAgent (TEA) (Ku et al., 2025) and Code2Video (C2V) (Chen et al., 2025), which serves as a vision-centric baseline that employs a VLM as a judge agent to provide feedback on rendered frames. Benchmark and Backbones.We utilize the MMMC-Code benchmark (Chen et al., 2025), containing 117 complex instructional topics across calculus, linear algebra, and physics. This benchmark is uniquely suited for SGA evaluation as it requires simultaneous optimization of pedagogical reasoning and precise geometric layout. blocks.text: Conclusion
heading_path: SGA: Plug&Play Geometric Verification for Educational Video Synthesis
Conclusion

blocks.text: We introduced the Symbolic Geometric Agent (SGA), a neuro-symbolic framework that addresses spatial blindness in code-centric generative pipelines by shifting layout refinement from perceptual inference to deterministic geometric verification. Evaluated on the MMMC-Code benchmark, SGA consistently improves programmatic video quality across multiple LLM backbones and agentic pipelines, achieving MVQS gains of up to 16.1% over the raw baseline while reducing refinement overhead with a 6×–18× per-iteration speedup. We also proposed MVQS, a deterministic metric for evaluating mathematical animation quality that captures spatial correctness overlooked by VLM-as-Judge aesthetics scores. Owing to its model-agnostic, plug-and-play design, SGA integrates easily into existing pipelines as a spatial guardrail or a deterministic alternative to perceptual layout critics. heading_path: SGA: Plug&Play Geometric Verification for Educational Video Synthesis
Limitations

blocks.text: Despite the significant improvements in spatial grounding provided by the SGA, several limitations remain. First, the current implementation is

blocks.text: specialized for 2D geometric primitives within the Manim engine; extending this to 3D scenes would require a more complex instrumentation of cameraspace projections and depth-sorting. Second, while the SGA resolves physical overlaps, it does not currently address temporal synchronization issues (e.g., ensuring a label appears exactly when a shape is drawn). Finally, the MMMC-Code benchmark is restricted to English-language mathematical content, and future work is required to evaluate the framework’s robustness across diverse linguistic and pedagogical traditions. Additionally, MVQS has not yet been validated against human expert annotations; such correlation analysis remains an important direction for future work.

blocks.text: Ethics Statement
heading_path: SGA: Plug&Play Geometric Verification for Educational Video Synthesis
Ethics Statement

blocks.text: We acknowledge several ethical considerations regarding the deployment of the SGA. While the framework guarantees geometric integrity and visual clarity, it does not verify the mathematical or pedagogical truth of the underlying theorems generated by the LLM. Users must be aware that a visually "perfect" and overlap-free animation can still contain factual inaccuracies. Furthermore, high performance on the MVQS metric could induce an automation bias, leading educators to bypass manual verification of the content. We mitigate these risks by positioning the SGA as an assistive guardrail for human-in-the-loop content creation. Finally, we disclose that AI assistants were utilized during the drafting phase of this manuscript for prose refinement and code optimization.

blocks.text: Three findings are noteworthy. First, Ssp and Sly are empirically independent ( ρ=−0.030 , n.s.), indicating that spatial separation does not systematically reduce layout density in practice, and validating the additivity assumption underlying the weighted sum: the sub-scores measure largely orthogonal aspects of layout quality. Second, the only significant inter-component dependency is Sly–Sed (ρ=−0.577 , p= 0.003 ): denser layouts increase annotation collision risk and thereby penalize Sed. This reflects an inherent property of the design space rather than a metric artifact. Third, the composite MVQS is primarily driven by Ssp and Sed (ρ= +0.680 ∗∗∗ and +0.692∗∗∗, respectively), confirming that the published weighting (wsp = 0.5 , wed = 0.3 ) correctly prioritizes the sub-scores most sensitive to educational spatial quality. The negative Sly–MVQS correlation (ρ=−0.286 , n.s.) is consistent with the Sly–Sed dependency: configurations with higher layout density tend to have more annotation collisions, depressing Sed and thereby the composite, even when Sly itself rises. The effect is non-significant and does not affect the rank-stability conclusions.

blocks.text: Relationship to Human Perception
heading_path: SGA: Plug&Play Geometric Verification for Educational Video Synthesis
Relationship to Human Perception

blocks.text: MVQS is an engineering proxy grounded in geometric axioms rather than a direct substitute for human judgment. Its atomic components (Sovlp, Sbound, Sleg) correspond to layout violations that graphic-design guidelines and educationalmedia research identify as primary readability barriers (Mayer, 2002; Sweller, 1994). Empirical validation of thecompositeagainst expert annotation remains future work. However, the cross-metric analysis in Section 4.2 of the main paper, provides a partial bridge: the educational sub-score Sed correlates significantly with the VLM-Judge Educational Logic dimension (ρ= +0.58, p= 0.003), the only perceptual dimension that overlaps with MVQS’s intended scope. The remaining sub-scores ( Ssp, Sly) are deliberately designed to detect violations that perceptual critics miss, so a low correlation with VLM dimensions is expected rather than a validity threat.

blocks.text: SGA’s fault-tolerant execution strategy wraps each statement in the Manim construct() method in a try-except block, allowing the pipeline to continue past runtime errors. A natural question is whether this strategy silently drops objects that would otherwise cause collisions, artificially inflating spatial scores. We address this by reporting the scene-level completion ratio η=N ok/Nprocessed, where Nprocessed is the number of scenes submitted to the pipeline and Nok is the number successfully evaluated. blocks.text: Both SGA and the VLM Critic were evaluated under a fixed budget of n= 1 refinement iteration applied identically across all pipeline/backbone combinations. For each topic, the procedure is: (1)

blocks.text: generate initial script C(0) with backbone L; (2) apply one round of feedback (SGA or VLM Critic); (3) generate refined script C(1) with the same backbone L; (4) evaluate C(1) with both MVQS and VLM-Judge. The SGA scene counts in Table 6 are exactly 2× the RAW counts for every backbone (e.g., 288 vs. 144 for GPT-5.1), providing direct empirical confirmation that each topic was processed through exactly one generate–refine–evaluate loop. Both methods consume exactly one LLM inference call per iteration. The only asymmetry is the rendering cost: the VLM Critic requires a full rendering pass ( ≈30–90 seconds) before inference, whereas SGA uses partial execution (<5 seconds). This difference does not affect the number of refinement steps or the information available to the backbone during refinement; it affects only wall-clock latency, which is reported separately in Section 4.3 of the main paper.
